worksheet.title: Put It in Order
worksheet.subtitle: An algorithm is steps in the right order
worksheet.learning_goal: I can put the steps of a task in the right order.

parts.title: What is an algorithm?
parts.text: An algorithm is a set of steps you do in order to finish a job. These step-cards are mixed up. Read them, then put them in the right order so the job works. Imagine doing the task in your head to check your order.

parts.title: Number the steps
parts.prompt: Write 1, 2, 3, 4 on the cards above to show the right order to plant a seed. Think: what must Bit do first?

parts.title: Write the order
parts.prompt: Now write the letters in the right order in the boxes.

parts.title: You try — order it
parts.prompt: Number these cards 1 to 4 for washing hands, then write the letters in order in the boxes.

parts.title: Big idea
parts.text: An algorithm only works when the steps are in the right order. If two steps swap, the job can go wrong — like drying your hands before you wash them!

teacher_guide.title: Put It in Order
teacher_guide.subtitle: Quick facilitation notes & answer key
teacher_guide.footer_topic: 1. Put It in Order — Teacher Guide

parts.title: What this worksheet teaches
parts.text: Students put a set of mixed-up step-cards in the right order to make a task work (planting a seed, washing hands). Putting the steps of a task in order is making a plan — the everyday name for an algorithm. No coding experience needed.

parts.title: Before you start (no computer needed)
parts.text: No computer — paper and a pencil. You read each prompt aloud. Optional: cut the steps into cards so students can physically slide them into order before writing.

parts.title: How to lead it (about 20 minutes)
text: 1. Show them (you do). Read the planting cards aloud and ask: "what must Bit do first?" You cannot drop the seed before you dig the hole.
2. Do one together. Number the planting cards in order, then write the letters in the boxes.
3. Let them try. Students order the wash-hands cards on their own.

parts.title: Answer key (these are the verified correct answers)
text: Exercises 1 & 2 — Plant a seed: dig a hole (C), drop the seed (A), cover the seed (D), water it (B). Order: C, A, D, B.
Exercise 3 — Wash hands: wet hands (B), soap (C), rinse (D), dry (A). Order: B, C, D, A.
Why the order matters: each step needs the one before it. Swap two and the job fails (drying before washing leaves hands dirty).

parts.title: If students get stuck — and ways to adjust
text: Watch for: ordering cards by where they sit on the page. Ask "which one has to happen first?"
Make it easier: slide real step-cards into order by hand before writing.
Make it harder: ask them to explain why two of the steps cannot swap.

parts.title: Ontario curriculum link (official wording)
text: C3.1 — solve problems and create computational representations of mathematical situations by writing and executing code, including code that involves sequential events.
In plain terms: students put step-by-step instructions in the right order to get a result.
C3.2 — read and alter existing code, including code that involves sequential events, and describe how changes to the code affect the outcomes.
In plain terms: students read a set of steps, change or reorder one, and explain what the change did.

parts.title: You'll know it worked when
parts.text: The child orders both tasks correctly and can say why a step must come before another.
